title: From written rules to learning systems

sources.claim: IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a 1997 match, relying mainly on fast search and hand-crafted evaluation; DeepMind's AlphaGo, which used deep neural networks, beat Go champion Lee Sedol 4-1 in March 2016.

sections.skill: Explain the shift from written rules and search to learning from data

questions.domain: Society: history and claims about the future
questions.prompt: What did early AI often rely on?

choices.text: Large language models trained on most of the text on the internet, as modern chatbots are

questions.intro: Early AI often relied on HAND-WRITTEN RULES and SEARCH: people wrote rules, and programs searched through possibilities. IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a 1997 match, relying mainly on very fast search and evaluation methods crafted by experts. Over time, the field shifted toward LEARNING FROM DATA, where systems find patterns from examples. In March 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo, which used deep neural networks trained on data and self-play, beat Go champion Lee Sedol 4 games to 1. Go has far more possible positions, so search alone was not enough.

sections.skill: Compare rules and learning with two ways to learn cooking

questions.domain: Society: history and claims about the future
questions.prompt: The recipe-book cook is like which approach?
questions.intro: One cook follows a detailed RECIPE BOOK exactly: every step written by an expert. That works well for standard dishes but struggles with new ingredients. Another cook LEARNS BY TASTING thousands of dishes and noticing patterns, then improvises. That handles variety but may make surprising mistakes and cannot always explain why. Early AI was more like the recipe follower; much modern AI is more like the taster.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Use the history to predict failures

questions.domain: Society: history and claims about the future
questions.prompt: Did AlphaGo use only learning?

choices.text: No; it combined learned networks with search
Yes, it used only neural networks and did not search through any possible moves at all

questions.correct_answer: No; it combined learned networks with search
questions.intro: The shift was not a clean switch. Many systems combine rules, search and learning; AlphaGo itself combined learned networks with search. Rule-based systems are still useful where rules are clear and must be followed exactly, such as tax calculations. Learning systems shine where examples are plentiful but rules are hard to write, such as recognizing speech. Knowing which approach a system uses helps you predict how it will fail.
